title: What Career Emergence Actually Feels Like
author: Molly G.
summary: A former startup COO turned TED podcast host reflects on five years of unplanned career reinvention, arguing that career navigation without a fixed long-term plan is viable — and survivable — if you replace the map with a compass. She names three lessons: first, that abandoning a five-year plan requires substituting some other navigational principle, which she found in "joy" (the work she'd do even unnoticed); second, that not knowing where you're headed feels genuinely terrible, not charmingly experimental, and that the antidote is favoring reversible decisions and getting outside support rather than grabbing the first "life raft" to end the uncertainty; and third, that some opportunities — in her case, becoming host of TED's WorkLife podcast — are structurally impossible to plan for because they didn't exist yet, and only become visible in hindsight once the underlying pattern of small, energy-following choices has had time to accumulate. The piece is explicitly a companion to a more polished essay she wrote for Lenny's Substack, adding the emotional texture — regret, self-doubt, a coach who helped her tolerate not-knowing — that a retrospective survivorship narrative tends to omit.
points: Abandoning a fixed career plan doesn't mean abandoning navigation altogether — the author replaced her five-year plan with "joy" (the work she'd do even if no one noticed) as an explicit decision filter for what to pursue and what to stop.

Not knowing where you're headed is not charming in the moment — it felt "fucking terrible," with no external evidence (promotion, title, raise) confirming the direction was right, which is precisely when people are most tempted to grab a premature answer.

In the wandering phase, reversible decisions are an ally and permanent ones are a risk — a big, hard-to-reverse commitment made to escape uncertainty is more often "a temporary fix for your anxiety" than an actual destination.

Her biggest opportunity (hosting TED's WorkLife podcast) was, in her own words, "impossible" to have been in her five-year plan five years earlier — some outcomes only become visible in hindsight, after enough energy-following choices accumulate into a legible pattern.

Hiring a coach mattered specifically because the coach didn't try to resolve the uncertainty — she helped the author "stay in the wandering instead of trying to solve it," reframing the goal from eliminating ambiguity to tolerating it productively.
quotes: The career version is the idea that instead of trying to design your career toward a clear long-term plan, you can clarify your principles, focus on the right next step, and trust that something you could never have planned might emerge.
At some point, I started using the word "Joy" as my compass: the work I would want to do even if no one was noticing. That sounds slightly woo-woo, but it became incredibly practical.

The hardest part was that I had no external evidence that I was going in the right direction. There was no promotion or title or salary increase telling me, "Good job, keep going." I had to trust my own compass—which sounds lovely when I write it now and felt fucking terrible at the time.

It is so important to be wary of decisions that are a "one-way door" (hard to take back) in the wandering phase. Anything reversible is your friend; anything permanent might just be a temporary fix for your anxiety, not a long-term happy place.

That conversation eventually led to TED offering me the opportunity to take over as host of WorkLife, the podcast they'd built with Adam Grant over the previous seven years. WorkLife was not unlikely to be in my five-year plan. It was impossible to be in my five-year plan.

All I could do was pay attention to what gave me energy, say no when something felt wrong even when I couldn't fully explain why, and keep choosing the next step that felt right. And then, eventually, the pattern emerged.
